listings.name: Orquesta Nacional de España
listings.content: Tickets are sold at ticket offices in the Auditorio Nacional de Música, Teatro María Guerrero, Teatro de la Zarzuela, Teatro de la Comedia, and Teatro Valle-Inclán.

listings.name: Orquesta de la Comunidad de Madrid
Banda Sinfónica Municipal de Madrid
listings.content: Performs in El Retiro Park in the summer. Tickets can be purchased at the Teatro Monumental (listed above), at the tourist information centre in Plaza Mayor, and online.

listings.name: La Trashumancia
listings.content: Annual event during which the centre of Madrid is free of cars and is instead filled with shepherds exercising their ancient right to drive sheep and livestock through the city.

listings.name: Madrid Gay Pride
listings.content: Annual event held between the last week of June and the first of July, with more than 1.5 million people in the street from all around the world. It began as a weekend party, but lately turned into a full-week extravaganza.

listings.name: Calle Cava Baja
listings.content: This narrow street in La Latina is by far the most famous and popular place for tapas.

listings.name: Plaza de Cibeles
listings.content: A massive roundabout at the intersection of Calle de Alcala and Paseo del Prado, this plaza houses one of Madrid's emblems, the Fountain of Cibeles, which portrays the Roman goddess of fertility sitting upon a chariot pulled by two lions. On the southeast corner dominating the Plaza is one of the world's most beautiful city halls, the Palacio de Cibeles (formerly the Palacio de las Comunicaciones), an impressive structure with a jaw-droppingly spectacular façade. Inside, the building holds a cultural center with changing art exhibits and info on Madrid, and you can climb to the upper floors for some excellent views out the window. On the southwest corner of the square sits the imposing Bank of Spain (Banco de España) building, while the northeast corner is home to the Palacio de Linares, which holds the Casa de América, a cultural center with an art gallery of Latin American works.

listings.name: Museo del Prado
listings.content: One of the finest art collections in the world and the best collection of classical art in Madrid. It includes many different collections: the Spanish (El Greco, Velázquez, and Goya), the Flemish and Dutch (Rubens, van Dyck, and Brueghel), Italian (Botticelli, Tintoretto, Titian, Caravaggio, and Veronese) and German (Albrecht Dürer, Lucas Cranach, and Baldung Grien).Some highlights not to miss at the Prado include the Bosch masterpiece The Garden of Earthly Delights, Velázquez's masterpiece Las Meninas, the Black Paintings, The Third of May 1808, and a pair of paintings known as The Clothed Maja and The Naked Maja by Goya, Adoration of the Shepards by El Greco, and David with the Head of Goliath by Caravaggio. Be sure to walk along Paseo del Prado, a pedestrian walkway full of fountains and trees near the museum.Visitors can bypass the often extremely long queues by purchasing tickets beforehand by phone or online, for an additional €.90 fee per ticket. Tickets purchased online can be printed or downloaded onto a smart phone; all pre-purchased tickets can be picked up (with a reference number) or presented at the main (Jerónimos) entrance in the northeast corner of the building. If you are planning to spend a full day at the museum, it is possible to leave (e.g. for lunch) and reenter by getting your ticket stamped at the 'Educación' counter just inside the main entrance.An affordable café and cafeteria-style restaurant are on the ground floor, along with a gift shop. No food, drinks, backpacks or umbrellas are permitted (a bag check is just inside the main entrance). Photography not permitted.
listings.price: €15 (adults), €7.50 (seniors 65+), free (children/students under 25); free admission within 2 hours of closure; additional obligatory fee for special exhibits

listings.name: Museo Nacional Centro de Arte Reina Sofía
listings.content: Housed in a former public hospital with an adjacent modern wing, this museum contains Spain's largest collection of 20th century art. Created to house Pablo Picasso's renowned Guernica, allowed after the return of democracy to Spain, the work was initially behind armoured glass. That's gone, but you are kept further away from it that anywhere else in the gallery, and another room includes some Picasso etchings that were damaged in a 1971 political attack.The Reina Sofía also houses masterpieces by other Spanish masters including Joan Miró, Salvador Dalí, Juan Gris, and others, as well as works by a number of international artists, including Vasily Kandinsky, Paul Klee, Francis Bacon, and more.Purchasing tickets in advance no longer gives you a discounted entry but is a way to beat the queues. During free admission periods, it is still required to pick up a ticket at the ticket office; these times are especially busy and it is best to arrive a bit before the free period actually begins. Photography is permitted, except for the work of Oskar Schlemmer (even though he died in 1943). Backpacks are not permitted, but there are free lockers after both entrances (in the older and modern wings).
listings.image: Madrid - Extensión del Museo Nacional Centro de Arte Reina Sofía (MNCARS) 05.JPG

listings.name: Museo Thyssen-Bornemisza
listings.content: Contains a large art collection including masterpieces by Monet, Goya, Degas, Renoir, Van Gogh, Picasso, Mondrian, Bacon and Lichtenstein.
listings.price: €13 (adults), €9 (concessions), free (children under 12) and all at certain times (see website)
listings.image: Site of the Retiro and the Prado in Madrid 49 (29684554308).jpg

listings.name: CaixaForum Madrid
listings.content: A private centre particularly well-known for the 'vertical garden' by Patrick Blanc installed on a wall in front of the museum, as well as the quite special architecture of the building itself. The vertical garden can be seen from the street outside, just a block south of the Thyssen-Bornemisza and across from the Prado. The museum only displays temporary exhibitions, usually of a very high quality, in fields ranging from archaeology to contemporary art and architecture.
listings.price: €6, free (La Caixa account holders), free on 15 May, 18 May, 9 Nov

listings.name: Museo Naval de Madrid
listings.content: A beautiful museum with a large interesting collection about Spanish naval history, from the efforts of kingdoms of Aragon and Castilia, the many successes and few failures (what's known in English as the defeat of the Spanish Armarda has a section) in the 15th-17th centuries, the drastic decline in the 19th century and its consequences in terms of losing the country's empire, the division of the navy into opposing sides in the 1930s Civil War, to today. It's almost all labelled in English as well as Spanish. A temporary exhibition traces today's Spanish flag from its origin as the navy's attempt to have one that contrasted well with other navy's flags, and the museum has the very large flag flown by the Spanish flagship at the Battle of Trafalgar (the loss is blamed on the French admiral for insisting on sailing out of Cadiz to fight it!)

listings.name: Museo Nacional de Antropología
listings.content: Small but interesting museum with artefacts and models from the indigenous people of Asia (mainly the Philippines, former colony of Spain), Africa and America. The exhibits are described in Spanish; however, on each floor, there is a leaflet in English explaining all sections.
listings.price: €3 (adults), €1.50 (concessions), free (seniors/students/children under 18); free Sa after 14:00 and Su

listings.name: Parque del Retiro
listings.content: The main park of Madrid, the perfect place to take a rest during a sunny day, or take part in the drum circles around the statue of Alphonso XII on summer evenings. There is a large boating lake where one can hire a rowing boat - great fun for the children! There is a monument to the victims of the Madrid 3/11 terrorist bombings, the Forest of the Absent, and the Crystal Palace, a large structure entirely made of glass. Sunday afternoons in summer are a treat in the park, where young hippies play bongos and dance.
listings.image: Avenida de mejico parque del buen retiro.jpg

listings.name: Real Jardín Botánico de Madrid
listings.content: Established in 1755, the garden has been in its current location since 1774. Its extensive collection is dispersed over seven sections, five greenhouses, and a herbarium. A map of the garden is available here.
listings.address: Pl. Murillo, 2, Retiro. Close to Museo Nacional del Prado.

listings.name: Banda Sinfónica Municipal de Madrid
listings.content: An orchestra that performs in El Retiro Park in the summer. Tickets can be purchased at the Teatro Monumental (listed above) and at the tourist information centre in Plaza Mayor, as well as online.

listings.name: Museo del Jamón
listings.content: Tapas restaurant

listings.name: 100 Montaditos
listings.content: Tapas restaurant

listings.name: Las Adelitas Restaurante Mexicano
listings.content: Mid-range Mexican restaurant with an extensive range of authentic options, though do be aware the food portions are a lot larger than you would typically expect. The primary chef is from Oaxaca.

listings.name: FoggBar Birras & Burgers
listings.content: You can have 2 litres of sangría in a self service dispenser from just €14, or €13 for 2 litres of beer, and you get a free plate of patatas bravas. They also have a delicious selection of bocatas from €2.45. Big TV to watch the football matches while enjoying eating and drinking. If you say you've read this, they'll invite you to a glass of rosado wine.

listings.name: Kapital
listings.content: Enormous club with 7 floors. However, despite its popularity this club is usually not worth visiting. The owner has a policy to try to limit the number of foreigners in the club so if you are from anywhere except Spain, you will likely get bad treatment.

listings.name: Petit Palace Lealtad Plaza
listings.content: Stylish 4 star-hotel in the Retiro district in central Madrid.

listings.name: Puerta del Sol
listings.content: This plaza is the heart of Madrid and one of the busiest places in the city - a hub for the local transit system, a favorite meeting spot for locals, a visible area for festivals or political demonstrations, and an opportune location for tour guides, street performers, pickpockets and anyone else looking to take advantage of all the tourists on-hand. In the center of the plaza sits the Statue of King Charles III on horseback, facing the Royal Post Office (Real Casa de Correos), the red-and-white building adorned with a clock tower on the plaza's south side. The building served as Madrid's first post office, then the police headquarters under Franco before being transformed into its current use as the office of the President of Madrid, the head of the regional government. The clock tower is noteworthy for being the center focus of New Year's celebrations every year, which are broadcast across Spain and mark the traditional eating of the Twelve Grapes (one for each ring of the bell) and the beginning of a new year. In front of the building is Kilometer Zero (Kilómetro Cero), a plaque showing the point where the measuring of national highway system begins. On the east side of the plaza is the famous Bear and the Madroño Tree Statue, a bear climbing a madroño tree, which is the symbol of Madrid, and on the west side of the plaza is the Mariblanca statue, a white marble goddess of at least the 17th century. Nearby the giant neon Tío Pepe sign sits above the plaza and is a famous fixture of this area.

listings.name: Gran Vía
listings.content: Literally 'Great Way' (better translated as 'Broadway'), Gran Vía is one of the busiest avenues in Madrid. Running from Plaza de España to Plaza de Cibeles, it is the location of the cinema district and a number of shopping malls and is lined with large billboards and lights. There's a constant buzz of traffic and life – 03:00-04:00 early morning traffic jams are not unusual.

listings.name: Real Academia de Bellas Artes de San Fernando
listings.content: Highly impressive art collection with paintings, sculptures, drawings and prints. Several Goya masterpieces.
listings.price: €10 (adults), €5 (seniors/students over 25), free (students/children under 18); free on W and national holidays
listings.image: Palacio de Goyeneche - Real Academia de Bellas Artes de San Fernando.jpg

listings.name: La Tabacalera
listings.content: An abandoned tobacco factory turned into a huge Berlin-like alternative art space driven by the diverse locals of Lavapies district. Also free workshops daily. Nice big cheap outdoors terrace.It is hoped that the closure is temporary and that it will return in a reduced form after works, check website for current situation.

listings.name: Auditorio 400
listings.content: The main venue for contemporary music, dance, and theatre performance.

listings.name: Círculo de Bellas Artes
listings.content: A non-profit cultural center located a short walk from Sol, the CBA offers up a wide variety of events and shows including film, music, art displays, dance, theater and more. See the website (in Spanish) for a list of activities. Great panoramic views of the city can be had from the Azotea, located at the top of the building.

listings.name: Cardamomo Tablao Flamenco
listings.content: Authentic Flamenco show in the center of Madrid, one of the greatest tablaos flamencos all over Spain, typical Spanish food during the performance.

listings.name: Teatro de la Zarzuela
listings.content: The Spanish version of the operetta (zarzuela) is performed here. This is also the main concert venue for the Community of Madrid Orchestra.
listings.image: Teatro de la Zarzuela Madrid auditorio 1.jpg

listings.name: Orquesta de la Comunidad de Madrid
Orquesta Sinfónica de RTVE
listings.content: Performs every Th and F at the Teatro Monumental on Calle Atocha.

listings.name: Yelmo Cineplex Ideal
listings.content: Probably the best known V.O. (versión original, or original language) theatre in Madrid, it offers the largest selection of movies and is a short walk from Sol.

listings.name: Cine Doré
listings.content: This is a wonderful old Spanish theatre dating from the 1920s. It has three screens and shows mainly art-house and critically acclaimed films in the original language. In the summertime, they screen movies on the roof.

listings.name: Essential Flamenco
listings.content: An authentic flamenco show in the heart of Madrid, set in a traditional exposed brick cave of the XIX century. Daily shows at 18:00, 19:30 and 21:00. Free drink included.

listings.name: Cervecería 100 Montaditos
listings.content: Branch of the popular nationwide chain that offers 100 different montaditos (small sandwiches). Great place to go for a cheap drink and bite to eat. Further branches are at Calle de la Montera, 34 (near metro Gran Vía) and Plaza de las Cortes, 3.

listings.name: Museo del Jamón
listings.content: One of several branches of this chain. Offers deli takeout service as well as tapas and raciónes at reasonable prices. They offer €1 ham sandwiches and a 'picnic' lunch consisting of a said ham sandwich, fresh fruit and a drink for €2 (Feb 2017). Another branch is at Calle de Atocha, 54 (metro Antón Martín).

listings.name: Casa Toni
listings.content: Very solid local option for small dishes/tapas. Recommended are chorizo, pig ears, tortilla with chorizo (omelette with chorizo), morcilla, sepia a la plancha. Casual non pretentious place.

listings.name: Matador
listings.content: Fantastic little stop for tapas. A very cozy place with good tapas and they always treat you very well. With a funny decoration.

listings.name: Takos Al Pastor
listings.content: Good taqueria. The tacos are amazing. The quesadillas and tortas are also worth it. The queue seems super long, but it moves fast.

listings.name: Puerto Rico
listings.content: Small little cantine with excellent and satisfying authentic Spanish food. You have to queue, but it's quite fluid and it's worth it.

listings.name: Mercado de San Fernando
listings.content: Lively market that has not been completely swamped by tourism. Wide range of food & drink available. (including Vegan)

listings.name: Alhambra
listings.content: This is a good place to drop by on a hot afternoon to enjoy a cold beer and some Andalusian tapas. Sample the sausages and cheeses.

listings.name: La Casa del Abuelo
listings.content: A Madrid landmark in operation for over 100 years, this bar attracts a standing room only crowd on the weekends. They mainly serve shrimp-based tapas dishes so if you're not into shellfish it may be advisable to steer clear. Order a plate of their garlic shrimp and accompany with their house wine.
listings.image: Casa del abuelo gambas a la plancha.jpg

listings.name: El Inti de Oro
listings.content: For something different, try this great Peruvian restaurant a short walk from Sol. Be sure to order some of their ceviche and try the Pisco Sour cocktail.

listings.name: Viva Chapata
listings.content: All-vegan restaurant that doesn't compromise on flavor, a good place to try vegan versions of Spanish tortilla and croquetas.

listings.name: Café Central
listings.content: Café by day, live jazz music at night.

listings.name: La Mallorquina
listings.content: Famous for its pastries. Peaceful upstairs room where you can linger undisturbed over your café con leche and napolitana de chocolate (chocolate croissant).

listings.name: Nuevo Café Barbieri
listings.content: Slightly scruffy cafe draws an avante garde crowd at night.

listings.name: La Pecera del Círculo de Bellas Artes
listings.content: A soaring hall on the ground floor of Madrid's art center combines atmosphere, excellent food and good coffee at reasonable prices. A wonderful place for lunch not far from Madrid's shopping or museums.
listings.image: Churros at the Círculo de Bellas Artes.jpg

listings.name: Museo Chicote
listings.content: Voted the Best European Bar 2004 by MTV-Campari. Extensive cocktail list. Claims to have served drinks to many famous celebrities, including, Ava Gardner, Frank Sinatra, Lana Turner, Gary Cooper, Orson Wells, Yul Brynner and Ernest Hemingway, Catherine Zeta Jones, Hugh Grant and Tim Robbins. They only serve drinks.

listings.name: Dubliners
listings.content: An Irish bar in the centre of Madrid near Puerta del Sol. The bar has televisions and is one of the places where sport can be seen.

listings.name: Xaloc Bar de Copas
listings.content: Discopub in the core of Barrio de las Letras. Great place with excellent prices but a good quality. The bar includes nice music, a DJ, and a moderately large dance floor.

listings.name: Viva Madrid
listings.content: Opened in 1856, this Madrid institution is known for its old-world charm and its creative takes on tapas and cocktails. José Rizal, the Philippines' national hero, was a regular patron, with a plaque hanging above the door in his honor.
listings.address: Calle de Manuel Fernández y González, 7

listings.name: Chinaski Lavapiés
listings.content: Interesting mixture of unusual local and foreign beers.

listings.name: El Sol
listings.content: Popular with the 20-30 age group. Plays a mix of 70s, funk, and bossanova sounds. No dress code, but people do tend to look cool.

listings.name: Ohm
listings.content: Popular Commercial House club with a mixed young straight/gay crowd.
listings.address: Plaza de Callao, 1 (in Gran Via street)

listings.name: Stardust
listings.content: Powerful Techno/House club popular within the younger crowd.

listings.name: Mad Hostel
listings.content: Nice, clean, quiet weekend hostel. 5 minutes from metro, tapas and services. 10-minute walk to Puerto del Sol, museums and Gran Via. Close to southern 'ethnic' areas = good food. Big common room with 4 computer stations, unreliable Wi-Fi and good free breakfast. Secure locker with every bed.

listings.name: Cat's Hostel
listings.content: Located in a 17th-century palace, but has a modern interior and is clean and secure. Breakfast and internet is included in the price and there is also a bar. It attracts a young backpackers clientele, but the crowd here is such that you're more likely to find partiers than hitchhikers. Shared dormitories for 4 to 14 people.

listings.name: Way Hostel Residence
listings.content: Small hostel, nice ambiance and is catered to young travelers. Nice kitchen, friendly staff, and free internet.

listings.name: Hostal San Martin
listings.content: Small, clean guest-house on the 4th floor. Ideally located just meters from Gran Via, with great staff and free WI-fi. All rooms have sink & shower, but most share bathrooms.

listings.name: Hotel ibis Styles Madrid Prado
listings.content: The small and inconspicuous ibis Styles gets great reviews thanks to a combination of nice rooms, good staff and ideal location, all that at a reasonable price including breakfast.

listings.name: Hostal Plaza d'Ort
listings.content: Cheap hotel with a good location near Plaza de Santa Ana. All rooms feature bathrooms, TV and air conditioning.

listings.name: ibis budget Madrid Centro Lavapies
listings.content: Budget hotel convenient for metro station. Some single rooms.

listings.name: Artistic Bed & Breakfast
listings.content: In the center of Madrid, a quiet bed and breakfast with a unique style and decoration.

listings.name: Asturias
listings.content: A 2-star hotel. The Asturias is 200 meters from the central Puerta del Sol.

listings.name: Hotel Madrid Preciados
listings.content: 4-star hotel in excellent location.

listings.name: Hotel Senator Gran Via Madrid
listings.content: 4-star hotel. Restaurant, bar, and meeting space.

listings.name: ME Madrid Reina Victoria
listings.content: Located in Plaza de Santa Ana.

listings.name: Hotel De Las Letras
listings.content: Old building with tasteful modern interior. Well sound-proofed against the busy Gran Via outside. Very comfortable beds. Rooms with TV, hi-fi, mini bar, bath/shower. Optional breakfast buffet with wide choice of good quality food and drinks. Pleasant, comfortable bar.

listings.name: Maria Elena Palace
listings.content: The Hotel María Elena Palace is located just 200 metres away from the Puerta del Sol. Renowned for its magnificent glass dome in the lobby.

listings.name: Hotel Quatro Puerta del Sol
listings.content: The turn-of-the-century grandeur with modern conveniences and amenities. Hotel Quo Puerta del Sol is housed in an emblematic building from the beginning of the 20th century with unique views of the city. It was totally restored in 2003.

listings.name: Museo de Historia de Madrid
listings.content: This museum is dedicated to the history of Madrid from 1561 to present. Much of the history is explained by referencing exhibited paintings depicting people or events from the time, so it is also an art museum. Several maps and models (including two large ones in the basement) show how Madrid grew since the 16th century. All exhibits are explained in both English and Spanish.

listings.name: Plaza del Dos de Mayo
listings.content: Central square of the Malasaña neighbourhood. It was named after the 2 May uprising of 1808 against the Napoleonic occupation of Spain. A monument in its centre honours the leaders of the uprising who were executed. The monument is Malasaña's symbolic landmark that is pictured on Malasaña postcards, on the label of Malasaña beer and other local merchandise.
listings.image: Plaza del Dos de Mayo, Madrid.jpg

listings.name: Palacio Longoria
listings.content: Exceptionally ornamental art nouveau building, erected 1902–03 for the banker and politician Javier González Longoria. It was designed by the Catalan architect Jose Grasses Riera and is considered to be one of the most important and beautiful examples of Spanish modernismo. Today, it houses the Spanish society of authors and editors. It can only be visited from the outside, but you may cast a glance at the entrance hall and staircase.

listings.name: Cuartel del Conde-Duque
listings.content: This former military building now not only serves as a venue for musical, dance, and theatrical performances but also hosts contemporary art exhibits. Tickets for performances are also sold online.

listings.name: Mercado de San Ildefonso
listings.content: Streetfood market on Fuencarral street, right in the middle of the Malasaña-Chueca area. 15 different stalls offer arepas (cornmeal griddlecake), brochetas (skewer), tacos, tapas, ham, meats, wine, beer etc. Between late-May and early-June an international street food festival is celebrated.

listings.name: Antigua Huevería
listings.content: The very best huevos rotos ('broken eggs') and croquetas. Cheap, beautiful and delicious! The chicken-adorned tiled front dates from the 19th century.

listings.name: Cervecería 100 Montaditos
listings.content: Popular nationwide chain that offers 100 different types of montaditos (small sandwiches). Great place to go for a cheap drink and bite to eat.

listings.name: Home Burger Bar
listings.content: THE place for serious hamburgers. Americans will feel at home!

listings.name: Home Burger Bar
listings.content: A second branch of the same concept.

listings.name: Tapería de Malasaña
listings.content: Taperia with lunch room out the back. Reviews mixed about the tapas but great place for lunch; they do a great Cocido Madrileño and the house wine is more than acceptable (although served somewhat cold).
listings.address: Calle Corredera Alta de San Pablo 8

listings.name: MAD MAD Vegan
listings.content: All plant based, mainly burger menu but with a few other items. If you like beer, their own craft bottled beers are good. English menu available.

listings.name: La Cocina del Desierto
listings.content: This dark, cave-like Moroccan restaurant has some of the best North African food in the city. The seating is at low Moroccan-style tables and the calm, mellow atmosphere makes you feel like you're far from the bustling center of Chueca.

listings.name: Lamucca de Pez
listings.content: Nice designer restaurant popular within the 20s-30s crowd. Good music, cool people, even better food and cocktails. The kitchen opens in the afternoon.

listings.name: La Panza es Primero
listings.content: This is a small, usually crowded, friendly Mexican restaurant with good food and drinks at reasonable prices. Sample some of their tacos and super-cheesy chilaquiles.

listings.name: Restaurante La Barraca
listings.content: Recommended for paella if a more authentic experience is sought.

listings.name: Restaurante Siam
listings.content: Beautifully-decorated with a tranquil atmosphere, the food is reasonable and offers a pleasant departure from Spanish fare, if so desired.

listings.name: El Tigre
listings.content: Probably the most well-known tapas bar in Madrid, a must do. Don't get frightened by how crowded the bar is and go in anyway. This is one of the most lively places in the city! Get beers, big glasses of wine or un mini de mojito and get free big plates of tapas every time you order. Very affordable.

listings.name: Café Comercial
listings.content: Opened in the 1880s, this is the oldest cafe in Madrid, and has been run by the same family since the early 1900s. There's a modern internet café upstairs, but the downstairs remains traditional.

listings.name: Pastelería La Duquesita
listings.content: Long-standing confectionery (established 1914), offering excellent tartlets that are not only delicious but also look picture-perfect. They are also sold to take away.

listings.name: Café Gijón
listings.content: A historic literary cafe. The outdoor terraza is nice in the summer.

listings.name: Café Restaurant El Espejo
listings.content: Opened in 1978, but looks much older. Has two divisions: a more casual café and a restaurant. Good food and very crowded during lunchtime.
listings.price: Café: €14-15 (midweek set menu), €19-20 (weekend set menu); Restaurant: set menu €11-17

listings.name: Libertad 8
listings.content: Libertad 8 is an iconic coffee shop and bar located on Libertad del barrio de Chueca, in Madrid. Opened as a coffee shop in 1975, ever since then it's served as a stage for artists and singer-songwriters (known as cantautores). It's become one of the most important spaces for songwriters, with frequent concerts by Pedro Guerra, Rosana, Ismael Serrano, Luis Pastor, Tontxu, Andrés Suárez, Lichis, Carlos Chaouen, or Kiko Tovar.

listings.name: L'Orangerie & Creperie
listings.content: Café, crêperie (place making crepes), sweets and very friendly staff – a good place for lovers of desserts and the sweet.

listings.name: Areia
listings.content: Very cool chill out bar decorated with deep colours in a Moroccan style. Dark and inviting. The seating includes cushions on the floor, traditional tables and chairs, or if you’re lucky, grab the four poster bed at the back.

listings.name: La Via Lactea
listings.content: A swingin' bar where you can twist the night away with local hipsters.

listings.name: Bee Beer
listings.content: Cosy craft beer bar with their own range of beers

listings.name: Demode
listings.content: Cool electronic sounds for 20s-30s.

listings.name: El Junco Jazz Club
listings.content: Smallish venue, starts the night with live jazz, later on morphs into relaxed night club. Not cheap (once inside, beer still €5.50, mixed drink €8.50), so attracts older crowd than others nearby.

listings.name: Hostal Jemasaca-Palma61
listings.content: Breakfast (coffee + pastry + juice) is included in price and it's served in a cafe near hostel. The nearest metro station is Noviciado. The room includes own bathroom and TV. Quiet and clean basic hostel.

listings.name: Hostal San Martin
listings.content: Small, clean guest-house on the 4th floor. Ideally located just meters from Gran Via, with great staff and free wi-fi. All rooms have sink & shower, but most share bathrooms.

listings.name: Hostal MH Fuencarral
listings.content: Centrally located, all rooms include bathroom, TV, free wi-fi, air conditioning, central heating, laundry and baggage storage facilities. Rooms with kitchen, washing machine and fridge are also available.

listings.name: Hostal Visa
listings.content: Simple, clean and secure. Central location close to Gran Via. Friendly staff.

listings.name: Hostal Asunción
listings.content: Simple but clean, on 2nd floor of building. Staff speak excellent English, very friendly. Reception open 6:00 to 00:00, but no curfew, guests get access code to front door. Good free WiFi.

listings.name: Hostal Pizarro
listings.content: Small hotel a short walk from Gran Via.

listings.name: Plaza Mayor
listings.content: Perhaps the best known plaza in Madrid, this impressive square is now one of the main stops on any tourist visit. This enclosed square was built outside the city walls, and has played host to bullfights, markets, symphonies, tournaments and executions. Today it is ringed with tourist shops, cafes and restaurants. The statue of Philip III sits in the middle across from the Casa de la Panadería, a beautifully painted building with two towers on the north side of the square (not to be confused with the other building with two towers on the opposite side) which once served as the headquarters of the bakers' guild and now houses a tourist information office. Access to the square is via one of the many arcades which connect to the surrounding pedestrian streets.

listings.name: Palacio Real
listings.content: The Palacio Real is an enormous palace, one of the biggest in Europe, with scorching plains of concrete around it. Though it is the official residence of the King of Spain, the royal family does not actually reside here and it is generally used only for state ceremonies. The Royal Palace is considered to be one of the most emblematic and beautiful buildings in Madrid, not only for its location on a bluff overlooking the river valley but also for its architecture and the artistic treasures to be found in its rooms. A simple one-way tour of the palace (both self-guided and guided are available) takes you up the grand stairway and through the lavishly decorated state rooms with their elegant tapestries, frescoes, porcelain, carvings and added decor like china, silverware, medals, etc. From the courtyard you can access the Farmacia (Pharmacy), which contains hundreds of bottles of early medicines and a reconstructed laboratory, and the Real Armorial (Royal Armory), a two-story collection of medieval weapons and armor. Explanations in the armory are in Spanish only, so do not expect to understand much unless your know the Spanish names for all that medieval weaponry.The lines to get in are very long, especially on weekday evenings when the place is free – try to go early. Photography inside the palace is not allowed, but is permitted in the foyer and courtyard. Free storage lockers are available behind the ticket office.The Palace was built on the site of an Alcazar (a Muslim fortress) which had been used as a palace but burned down. It was one of the first major buildings by the new Bourbon dynasty and shows a departure from the earlier styles and tastes of the Habsburgs in evidence in other royal buildings in the area.
listings.price: Entry €11; guided tour additional €4; students and children €6; free (disabled/teachers/children under 5); free M-Th 16:00-18:00 (Oct-Mar) and 18:00-20:00 (Apr-Sep) for EU citizens, legal residents, and citizens of Latin American countries (valid ID/passport required)

listings.name: Catedral de la Almudena
listings.content: This massive cathedral faces the Palacio Real. Finished near the end of 20th century in the Neo-Gothic style, it is where the Princes of Asturias Felipe (current King Felipe VI) and Letizia were married in 2004. Especially noteworthy are the 5,000-pipe organ, a large painted 15th-century Gothic altarpiece, and the empty 12th-century coffin of Madrid's patron saint, Isidro. Like many cathedrals before it, construction took a while, being started in the 19th century while it was only inaugurated in 1992. The cathedral thus reflects a mixture of styles which sometimes harmonize and sometimes clash. One of the reasons for the late start of construction of a cathedral in the capital of one of the world's most catholic states was the power of the archbishops of Toledo who did not want to give up their ecclesiastical power to the upstart Madrid. Similarly the monarchy had moved its residence from Toledo to Madrid in part to escape the influence of the church and installing a bishop in Madrid (a requirement for a cathedral) seemed somewhat counter productive. The cathedral is also the site of many burials of important figures, including the daughter of Franco.

listings.name: Mercado de la Cebada
listings.content: Once a glass and iron market of the late 19th century, it is now a vaulted concrete building which still serves as a neighborhood market. Where it used to stand an annexed public swimming pool and sports facilities, it lies now an empty field, used and managed by a neighbor association.

listings.name: Plaza de la Villa
listings.content: The main square during the Middle Ages, as Calle Mayor (High Street) was the main street as well. It houses the former City Hall, the former Academy of Fine Arts, and the Archbishopric.

listings.name: Museo de San Isidro
listings.content: This is a museum of two parts. One part is dedicated to Saint Isidore the Laborer, while the other part is dedicated to the paleontology and archaeology of the region of Madrid from prehistory to 1561 (when Philip II made Madrid the seat of the court). Most of the exhibits are explained in both Spanish and English.

listings.name: Corral de la Morería
listings.content: One of the most famous flamenco tablaos in the world. It′s right in the heart of the city, and you can enjoy a full-fledged Spanish meal while you watch performances by renowned international flamenco music and dance artists.

listings.name: Teatro Real
listings.content: The main opera theatre in Madrid. Tickets can be purchased online here.

listings.name: La Bola Taberna
listings.content: A family-run restaurant operating since 1870 and serving traditional Madrileño cuisine. Reservations can be made online.

listings.name: Chocolatería San Ginés
listings.content: Specializing in chocolate con churros, this Madrid fixture is the perfect place to top off a night on the town. Also offers the usual assortment of coffees and teas.
listings.image: At San Gines again. One of the oldest chocolate con churros in Madrid (18761909709).jpg

listings.name: Restaurante Malacatín
listings.content: Serves typical Madrid cuisine.

listings.name: Casa Lucio
listings.content: Pricey but worth it. The Spanish Royal family sometimes entertain guests here and you may run into a few sports figures and movie stars. You should definitely book ahead on the weekends, and reservations are recommended even for the weekdays. Known for their cocido, their roasts and their huevos rotos.

listings.name: Restaurante Botín
listings.content: Opened in 1725, Botín is listed in the Guinness Book of Records as the oldest operating restaurant in the world. Once a favourite of Ernest Hemingway, the menu still delights with specialities including cochinillo (roast suckling pig) and cordero (roast lamb).

listings.name: Calle Cava Baja
listings.content: This narrow street in La Latina is by far the most famous and popular place for tapas. It is also the place to go for the traditional Sunday-noon "Vermouth Hour" (after mass or shopping on El Rastro flea market).

listings.name: The Sherry Corner
listings.content: Sherry-tasting available in 8 languages. Commentary by knowledgeable oenologists explaining the details of the history, elaboration methods and tasting notes for each of the wines, while inviting guests to combine them with tapas served at different market stalls.

listings.name: Café de Oriente
listings.content: Overlooks the Plaza Oriente and faces Palacio Real. Outdoor tables in summer, cozy indoor rooms in the cold months. Basement banquet room with a glass floor over ancient remains. Excellent food.

listings.name: La Corolla
listings.content: Specializes in delicious ‘tostas’ (small pieces of toast with different toppings) and avocado (aguacate), along with cañas (small beers).

listings.name: Joy
listings.content: Well known across Europe. Attracts at multi-national crowd. Popular with tourists as well as locals. It plays a mix of popular dance music. Every Thursday there is a Students Party.

listings.name: Los Amigos Backpackers Hostel
listings.content: Very central location. Breakfast is offered. There is a lounge area, a kitchen in which you are able to cook your own food, and a bar. The beds are clean, comfortable, and the staff are friendly.

listings.name: Meninas Hotel
listings.content: 4-star hotel in an exquisite historic building of the XIX century in the historic center of Madrid that has been transformed into a state-of-the-art boutique hotel. A classic atmosphere blended with modern decorative touches - a balance of unpretentious formality and well tempered cordiality.

listings.name: The Hat Madrid
listings.content: Good hostel located close to the Plaza Mayor. Breakfasts served in rooftop restaurant area. Luggage storage available.

listings.name: Museo Lázaro Galdiano
listings.content: This museum houses the stunning collection of Spanish entrepreneur José Lázaro Galdiano (1862-1947) and is considered to be one of the best private collections in Spain. Not only will you find works by Goya, Velázquez, El Greco and others - the museum is also filled with jewelry, furniture, sculpture and ceramics. It is located in Lázaro Galdiano's rather lavish former residence. This is an excellent museum that is usually not crowded and well worth the price of admission.
listings.price: €6 (adults), €3 (seniors/students/disabled), free (children under 12); free admission Tu-Sa 15:30-16:30 and Su 14:00-15:00

listings.name: Museo Arqueológico Nacional
listings.content: Don't let the sound of it frighten you. This large, well-designed museum opened again in April 2014 after several years of renovation works. It houses an incredible collection of archaeological finds from across the peninsula. It leaves the visitor with a sense of the chronology of civilization in Spain (Iberian, Phoenician, Greek, Roman, Visigoth, Arab, and into the modern age). The famous Dama de Elche, an Iberian (pre-Roman) goddess statue, is in this museum. There are also a few pieces from ancient Egypt and Mesopotamia.
listings.price: €3 (adults), €1.50 (concessions); free on Sa after 14:30, Su mornings, and national holidays

listings.name: Fundación Juan March
listings.content: A few blocks off high-end shopping street Calle Serrano, this private foundation houses free temporary exhibitions of (mostly 20th-century) art which are often worth checking out. 10-15 min walk from either Museo Lázaro Galdiano or National Archaeology Museum.

listings.name: Parque de El Capricho
listings.content: One of the most beautiful parks in Madrid. Built in 1797-1839, it has a strong Romanticism influence. Declared as an Historic Garden, its lakes with swans and ducks, labyrinths, palaces, squares and fountains makes this a lovely place.
listings.image: MADRID PARQUE DEL CAPRICHO EXEDRA VALIDA 3-12-2006.jpg

listings.name: Plaza de Toros de Las Ventas
listings.content: Arguably the most important bullfighting site in Spain. Unless you find this spectacle distasteful, this is a must see if you visit Madrid during the bullfighting season (May, during San Isidro). Tickets may nevertheless be expensive and hard to get for the more important corridas. Anyway, it usually is used as a venue for shows and concerts.
listings.image: Plaza de Toros de Las Ventas (Madrid) 03.jpg

listings.name: La Casa del Abuelo 3
listings.content: A third branch of the popular establishment.

listings.name: Estay Restaurante
listings.content: A great place for tapas, they offer a large menu, reasonable prices and excellent quality food. The solomillo al foie is excellent and the desserts come highly-recommended as well. Very crowded on Friday and Saturday nights.

listings.name: Bar Jaén III
listings.content: An excellent tapas bar and restaurant. A nice place to enjoy Spanish food and lifestyle without spending too much. Located in a business park in the far-east of the city, it's far from being a tourist trap and you can enjoy good food and true raciónes (portions). The pleasant owners are very willing to share stories about Madrid and Spain more generally. In summer time it has a superb terrace, within a stone's throw of the Olympic Stadium.

listings.name: La Trainera
listings.content: A Madrid institution for decades, Trainera is an excellent but somewhat pricey restaurant serving strictly seafood dishes. They have a great wine selection and the waiters can recommend different vintages that will complement the food. Try the carabineros (giant scarlet shrimp) or the rodaballo (turbot).

listings.name: Osuna
listings.content: A bit outlying, some 20 minutes metro ride to the central districts.

listings.name: Gran Hotel Velazquez
listings.content: The Gran Hotel Velázquez is a 4 star hotel located in the Salamanca district. This hotel has been providing stylish accommodation for over 50 years.

listings.name: Gran Meliá Fénix
listings.content: Distinguished by a grand and glowing white exterior; bathed in neo-classical design; an illustrious interior of flowing banisters, bold colors, and noble décor.

listings.name: Hotel Villa Magna
listings.content: A 5-star hotel on one of Madrid's most exclusive streets. 151 rooms and suites. The hotel is surrounded by landscaped gardens.

listings.name: Torres de Colón
listings.content: Eye-catching twin towers, constructed 1967–74. With 116 metres and height and 23 floors, they are among the highest buildings in Madrid.

listings.name: Plaza de Olavide
listings.content: Circular place and nice green space (thanks to the motorised traffic being directed through a tunnel), surrounded by an ensemble of colourful 19th-century residential buildings.

listings.name: Nuevos Ministerios
listings.content: The modern government complex had already been planned by the republican government before the Civil War, but it was only completed in 1942 under the Francoist rule. Its architectural style is Neoclassical. The ministries of public works and labour are seated here.

listings.name: Hospital de Maudes
listings.content: Former hospital complex, built in 1916 in an eclecticist style (similar to Palacio de Cibeles, that was designed by the same architects). It includes a church, Santa María del Silencio. The hospital was intended to serve the poorer classes, therefore nicknamed Hospital de Jornaleros ("hospital of day labourers"). After the Civil War it became a military hospital, before falling out of use in 1970. In the 1980s, it was acquired by the autonomous Community of Madrid, refurbished and has since then housed the council of public works as well as a library.
listings.image: Madrid - Hospital de Maudes, Parroquia de Santa María del Silencio 03.jpg

listings.name: Constitutional Tribunal
listings.content: Modern circular building from the early 1980s, designed by architects Bonet and Valdés.

listings.name: Plaza de Castilla
listings.content: On the north side of the city and bisected by Paseo de la Castellana, this plaza is in the center of Madrid's skyscraper district. A tall obelisk sits in the center of the plaza while the Gate of Europe (Puerta de Europa) towers, two slanted towers which frame the boulevard, are on the north side of the plaza. Taking the #27 bus, which runs along Paseo del Prado and Paseo de la Castellana and ends at Plaza de Castilla, will take you pass several Madrid highrises.

listings.name: Cuatro Torres
listings.content: Four sleek skyscrapers, constructed between 2004 and 2009. Standing 224 to 249 metres tall, they are the highest in Spain. From south to north, they are named Torre Cepsa, Torre PwC, Torre de Cristal, and Torre Espacio. In the latter, the embassies of Great Britain, Australia and Canada are seated.

listings.name: Monumento a Rizal
listings.content: Honors Filipino national hero José Rizal (1861-1896), a revolutionary who was executed by the Spanish in Manila. This is a replica of the more famous "Motto Stella", which is located near his execution site at Rizal Park. This replica was built and inaugurated in 1996, marking the 100 year anniversary of Rizal's death. In the decades since its inauguration, it's become an important landmark for Filipinos visiting Madrid, and is a great opportunity for all to learn a bit more about this era of Spanish history.

listings.name: Basílica La Milagrosa
listings.content: Church from the 1900s in Neo-Mudéjar and Gothic revival style, dedicated to Our Lady of Miracles.

listings.name: Museo Sorolla
listings.content: This museum is in what was the impressionist painter's house and features fine furniture and porcelain as well as his paintings.
listings.price: €3 (adults), €1.50 (concessions); free admission Sa after 14:00 and all day Su

listings.name: Estación de Chamberí
listings.content: Former metro station designed by architect Antonio Palacios (creator of the Palacio de Cibeles, Círculo de Bellas Artes and Hospital de Maudes). It was inaugurated in 1919, but closed in 1966, thereby becoming a "ghost station". Since 2008 it has been converted to a museum, exhibiting original counters, signs, maps and advertising posters from earlier ages.
listings.price: Free, booking from website (Spanish) linked from English site.

listings.name: Museo Nacional de Ciencias Naturales
listings.content: Contains a large collection of fossils and minerals, plus educational exhibits (some are described in English but many are in Spanish only). Has two parts open to visitors with separate entrances. The ticket is purchased at the main entrance and to visit the other part you need to exit from the main entrance, turn left and follow the building until you reach the second entrance. Your ticket will be checked again there so don't lose it.

listings.name: Museo Geominero
listings.content: Part of the Spanish Institute of Geology and Mining, this museum is dedicated to Geology (with a focus on Mineralogy) and Paleontology, containing an impressive collection of fossils and minerals discovered on the territory of Spain and abroad. Also contains educational exhibits, although all are described in Spanish only. The interior of the building is just as impressive and may be worth a quick tour even if you are not particularly interested in Paleontology and Mineralogy.

listings.name: Museo Nacional de Ciencia y Tecnología
listings.content: The main entry for this museum has been moved to Alcobendas
listings.image: Museo Nacional de Ciencia e Tecnoloxía-MUNCYT.jpg

listings.name: Auditorio Nacional de Música
listings.content: The main concert venue for the Spanish National Orchestra and the Madrid Symphony Orchestra, as well as the main venue for touring classical artists and orchestras.

listings.name: Orquesta Nacional de España
listings.content: Tickets are sold at ticket offices in the Auditorio Nacional de Música, Teatro María Guerrero, Teatro de la Zarzuela, Teatro de la Comedia, and Teatro Valle-Inclán.

listings.name: Real Madrid
listings.content: For football fanatics, a trip to the Santiago Bernabeu, the home of local club Real Madrid is not to be missed. Real Madrid is the most successful football club in Spain and Europe, having been crowned Spanish champions a record 32 times and European champions a record 11 times. Their biggest rivals by far are FC Barcelona, with which it contests matches known popularly as El Clásico at least twice a year. The rivalry between the two sides is by far the biggest in Spain and one of the most intense in the world, and stems from the longstanding traditional rivalry between the Spanish and Catalan speaking parts of Spain. As such, tickets for such matches often sell out very quickly. In case you arrive in Madrid on non-match periods, you can take a self-guided tour of the Santiago Bernabeu Stadium. It includes tours around the field, the dressing rooms, the Press Room and the Real Madrid Museum where the trophies and other memorabilia are kept. Without a loyalty card, the typical fees for adults is €35 (online, €38 at the ticket office). However, a few days before a match, the chances are you will not be able to take the full tour, but only a part of it, with at least the Real Madrid Museum, at a reduced price.

listings.name: Cines Dreams
listings.content: This cinema is located in a shopping mall known for its ice-skating rink. It is a great place where teenagers can hang out since the mall also has restaurants, bars, and shops.

listings.name: Home Burger Bar
listings.content: The place for serious hamburgers. Americans will feel at home!

listings.name: Restaurante Samm
listings.content: Best paella in Madrid, but only if you bring more than two people by order of the proprietor. Frequented mainly by locals, prepare to be stared at by the wait staff if you are from out of town.

listings.name: Casa Nemesio
listings.content: Seafood.

listings.name: El Telégrafo
listings.content: Arguably the best seafood in Madrid.

listings.name: Cervecería Oldenburg
listings.content: Craft beers & good selection of Belgian & German Beers

listings.name: Beerhouse Craftbeer Bar
listings.content: Craft beer bar with a mixture of local & foreign beers.

listings.name: Cervecería L'Europe
listings.content: Small beer hall with a small food selection.

listings.name: Safestay Madrid Central
listings.content: Hostel with private & shared rooms. chain with hostels in many large European cities.

listings.name: Caballero Errante
listings.content: 3 star hotel with modern features, clean rooms and helpful staff. Just over 1.5km walk from the Bernabeu Stadium.

listings.name: Pension Paquita
listings.content: Family-run.

listings.name: Eurostars Suites Mirasierra
listings.content: A modern luxury hotel located in prestigious residential district Mirasierra, overlooking the Sierra de Guadarama. Facilities include a fitness centre, free parking, and free Wi-Fi. The hotel is also home to the Restaurante Verdil.

listings.name: Plaza de España
listings.content: A prominent square on the northwest side of central district, adjacent to two of the tallest buildings in Madrid, erected under Franco's rule in the 1950s: the neo-Baroque Edificio España (the red and white one) and the more modern-styled Torre de Madrid (the taller, white one), both designed by the Otamendi brothers and standing 117 and 142 metres tall, respectively. The square contains a large fountain and a sculpture of Cervantes and his famous Don Quixote and Sancho Panza characters.

listings.name: Casa Gallardo
listings.content: Imposing and highly ornamental Art nouveau (or modernismo) building at the western corner of Plaza de España, designed by Federico Arias Rey and completed in 1914.

listings.name: Arco de la Victoria
listings.content: Francoist triumph arch erected 1950–56 to commemorate the Nationalist victory in the Battle of Ciudad Universitaria of the Civil War.

listings.name: Palacio de la Moncloa
listings.content: A rather nondescript complex of buildings on the outskirts of Madrid, since 1977 it has served as the official residence and workplace of the Prime Minister of Spain. Its name has since become synonymous with the Spanish government as a whole. Off-limits to the public for many years, in 2018 it was opened to guided visits during the summer only for Spanish citizens and foreigners resident in Spain. Registration is required to participate, and while the Prime Minister's Office announces available tour dates in advance on its website, slots are limited and run out very quickly.

listings.name: Faro de Moncloa
listings.content: A 92 high tower with an observation deck that you can access by elevator. In theory your visit is limited to 30 minutes, but you're likely to want to go down before the time is up.

listings.name: Museo de América
listings.content: An excellent museum that many tourists miss. Houses thousands of artifacts from the Americas. The exhibit displays objects from many native cultures from before European conquest to colonial times and beyond. Don't miss the Tesoro (Treasure) de los Químbayas, a collection of gold objects that was given as a gift by the Colombian government. Also of interest is the Tudela Codex, an Aztec law book from the 1500s. Beware: most explanations to the objects on display are in Spanish only.

listings.name: Museo del Traje
listings.content: Offers a wide selection of historical and more temporary costumes (from the early 1200s to now) which shows the aspects of different cultures and Spain. The museum also organizes many activities and events. The building itself won some architectural awards in the 1970s. The restaurant underneath the museum is fairly good. The museum is surrounded by sprawling gardens, replete with well maintained lawns and fountains, are a pleasant place to relax.
listings.price: €3 (adults), €1.50 (concessions), free (students/children/seniors); free on Sa after 14:30, all day Su, and national holidays
listings.image: Museo del Traje, fuente frente al museo, Madrid, España, 2015.JPG

listings.name: Real Ermita de San Antonio de la Florida
listings.content: This small church is famous for its murals, painted by Goya. It's also the mausoleum of the painter.
listings.address: C/ Glorieta San Antonio de la Florida, 5
listings.image: Ermita de San Antonio de la Florida Madrid.jpg

listings.name: Templo de Debod
listings.content: An Egyptian temple in one of Madrid′s most beautiful parks. Near the Royal Palace and Plaza de España, it was a present given by Egypt to Spain for its role in saving the temple of Abu Simbel from the floodwaters of Lake Nasser following the construction of the Aswan Dam in southern Egypt. A great place to watch the sunset. Usually a queue. Only 30 people allowed in the area at a time

listings.name: Rosaleda del Parque del Oeste
listings.content: The rose garden of Madrid, located in the same park as the Templo de Debod. If you like roses and are in Madrid when they have flowered, definitely worth a visit. The garden holds an international competition yearly.
listings.image: Vista de la rosaleda del parque del Oeste.jpg

listings.name: Casa de Campo
listings.content: The park at the rear of the Palacio Real which used to belong to the Royal family. Much of the park has been taken to smaller activity parks such as the Zoo but in general it's peaceful. From Moncloa you can take a teleferico (€5.90 return) across into the park.
listings.image: Casa de Campo Lago y vista.jpg

listings.name: Zoo Aquarium de Madrid
listings.content: See the pandas, pet the lemurs, watch the dolphin show, and enjoy the bird show.
listings.price: €22.95 (adults), €18.60 (seniors/disabled/children 3-7), free (children under 3); ticket prices are significantly cheaper if purchase online

listings.name: Las Tablas
listings.content: A very popular flamenco tablao located near the Plaza España metro station. The package consisting of a Flamenco show (at 21:00 or 22:00) with a candle-lit dinner and a glass of Sangria wine is truly a treat.

listings.name: Sala Arena
listings.content: National touring acts for rock and pop music.

listings.name: Kinépolis
listings.content: Outside the city, in the suburb of Pozuelo de Alarcon. The largest megaplex in the world by number of seats. Has 25 screens. The offer of movies shown in their original version is increasing.

listings.name: Yunie Kebab
listings.content: One of the oldest kebab restaurants in Madrid, it is reportedly a favorite of the Spanish royal family. Also offers other Lebanese specialties like kibbeh and mutabbal (a spicier baba ghanoush).

listings.name: La Esquina de Eusebio
listings.content: Trays of tapas are passed from one person to another in this typical bar of Madrid, absolutely not touristy but really worth it! And it's not so far from the centre.

listings.name: Casa España
listings.content: Cheap Breakfast: 2 Euro The nearest metro station is Plaza de España. Popular budget hostel in the city center. Free WiFi, linens included
listings.price: Dorm: from 7,99 Euro. Double rooms: from 10,99 Euro

listings.name: Parque Madrid Río
listings.content: The motorway that used to carve into the city and blight the banks of Río Manzanares, was banished into a tunnel, in a superlative urban landscaping project that cost some €4 billion. Nowadays, a unique 6-km-long landscape garden accompanies the river on both banks. For this project, 33 bridges were dedicated, which allow you to cross from one side to another whenever you want, as well as 5500 benches installed and 33,000 trees planted. The park is multifaceted, including flowerbeds, Baroque-style boxwood broderies, pine, cypress or bamboo groves, playgrounds, climbing garden, skatepark etc. Asphalted paths are ideal for cyclists and roller skaters, while pedestrians enjoy priority rights. Cafés, "beach bars" and kiosks provide sustenance.

listings.name: Planetario de Madrid
listings.content: Features several exhibits related to space exploration, two screens playing documentaries, an interactive area and, of course, the planetarium. Projections last 45 minutes each. Different ones play on different days, so check their website. All the exhibits are explained in Spanish only and the projections in the planetarium are also in Spanish.
listings.price: Entry is free but the sessions in the planetarium each have a cost of €3.60 for a regular ticket and €1.65 for a reduced ticket (children and seniors)

listings.name: Museo de Ferrocarril de Madrid
listings.content: Museum with four railway tracks, exhibiting a large number of steam, diesel and electric locomotives used in Spain in the 19th and 20th century. Also on display are several model railways. Exhibits are described in Spanish only.
listings.price: M-Th F before 14:00, holidays: €6 adult, €4 concession, free child under 4; F after 14:00, Sa Su €2.50

listings.name: Matadero Madrid
listings.content: Madrid's former main abattoir (matadero), an early 20th-century industrial brick compound in Arganzuela district, has been converted to an arts and cultural centre since the 2000s. It is intended to serve as a cross-disciplinary laboratory of contemporary arts, including studios, exhibition spaces, a theatre, an arthouse cinema, and a library, as well as a café. One of the preferred spots of the city's "artsy" crowd to meet. There are performances and other events almost every day.

listings.name: Sala La Riviera
listings.content: Another large venue for touring rock and pop bands.
listings.address: Paseo Bajo de la Virgen del Puerto, s/n

listings.name: Gruta '77
listings.content: Concerts everyday: pop, rock, and punk.

listings.name: Madrid Open
listings.content: Held in mid-May at La Caja Mágica.

listings.name: Freiduría de Gallinejas Embajadores
listings.content: Another classic tapas bar in Madrid, not for conservative stomachs. Their most popular tapas are two of the most typical and traditional dishes in Madrid: gallinejas and entresijos. A treat for adventurous palates and lamb-lovers.

listings.name: Café Ziryab Tablao Flamenco
listings.content: A Flamenco venue with daily shows at 21:30 by first line artists, in an intimate ambiance. Kind staff, nice drinks and tapas, personalized attention and the artists right in front of you.

listings.name: La Esquina de Eusebio
listings.content: Trays of tapas are passed from one person to another in this typical bar of Madrid, absolutely not touristy but really worth it. And it's not so far from the centre.

listings.name: Sol Hostel
listings.content: Rooms from 4 to 14 people, plus breakfast and internet (WIFI).

listings.name: Museo Nacional de Ciencias Naturales
listings.content: Contains a large collection of fossils and minerals, plus educational exhibits (some are described in English but many are in Spanish only). Has two parts open to visitors with separate entrances. The ticket is purchased at the main entrance and to visit the other part you need to exit from the main entrance, turn left and follow the building until you reach the second entrance. Your ticket will be checked again there so don't lose it.

listings.name: Plaza de Castilla
listings.content: On the north side of the city and bisected by Paseo de la Castellana, this plaza is in the center of Madrid's skyscraper district. A tall obelisk sits in the center of the plaza while the Gate of Europe (Puerta de Europa) towers, two slanted towers which frame the boulevard, are situated on the north side of the plaza. Taking the #27 bus, which runs along Paseo del Prado and Paseo de la Castellana and ends at Plaza de Castilla, will take you pass several Madrid highrises. North of the Plaza is the Four Towers (Cuatro Torres), four sleek new skyscrapers which are the tallest in Spain.

listings.name: Parque de El Capricho
listings.content: One of the most beautiful parks in Madrid. Built in 1797-1839, it has a strong Romanticism influence. Declared as an Historic Garden, its lakes with swans and ducks, labyrinths, palaces, squares and fountains makes this a lovely place.

listings.name: Spanish National Research Council Headquarters
listings.content: Headquarters of the largest public institution dedicated to research in Spain and the third largest in Europe. Not a real touristic place, and they would probably not let you in to take a photo of the building, but this is the main filming location of the Royal Mint of Spain in the Spanish Emmy winner TV show, Money Heist (La Casa De Papel).

listings.name: Palacio Real de El Pardo
listings.content: It was built as a hunting lodge for the Spanish royal family, and was commandeered by Francisco Franco to serve as his residence. Today it serves as the official guest house for foreign dignitaries visiting Madrid, and is also open to the public when not in use. Check out the vast collection of tapestries hanging from the palace walls, some of which were even designed by the painter Francisco Goya.

listings.name: Auditorio Nacional de Música
listings.content: The main concert venue for the Spanish National Orchestra and the Madrid Symphony Orchestra, as well as the main venue for touring classical artists and orchestras.

listings.name: Real Madrid
listings.content: They play soccer in La Liga, the top tier, and are the most successful football club not only in Spain but in Europe, having been Spanish champions 32 times and European champions 14 times. Their biggest rivals are FC Barcelona, and these twice-yearly El Clásico matches sell out quickly, as does El Derbi against local rivals Atlético de Madrid. Their stadium, the Santiago Bernabéu, has a capacity of 81,000. It's one km south of Chamartin railway station and has its own Metro stop. On non-match days you can take a self-guided tour, adult €25, which includes the pitch, dressing rooms, Press Room and trophy museum. On days close to matches there is reduced access & entry price but the museum remains open. (The women's team play in Liga F their top tier at Alfredo Di Stéfano Stadium towards the airport.) Real Madrid also runs a basketball team known as Real Madrid Baloncesto, which like its illustrious football counterpart is the most successful in Spain and Europe, having won a record 34 Spanish league titles and 10 EuroLeague titles.

listings.name: Atlético de Madrid
listings.content: They play in La Liga, the top tier, and are one of the most successful teams in Spain, having won both La Liga and the Copa del Rey on ten occasions. They were European Cup runners-up in 2014 and 2016 and won the UEFA Europa League in 2010 and 2012. Since 2017 their home ground is Estadio Metropolitano, capacity 67,700, also known as Wanda Metropolitano. It's 10 km east of city centre in San Blas district, with its own metro station. The women's team play in Liga F (their top tier) at CD Wanda in Alcalá de Henares northeast of the city.

listings.name: Home Burger Bar
listings.content: Other burger bars of this brand can be found in Malasaña-Chueca.

listings.name: Churrería La Andaluza
listings.content: Opened in the 1930s just beside the Mercado de Maravillas, this Tetuán institution is regarded as one of the best churrerías in Madrid, with freshly-made churros, porras and buñuelos (round, donut-shaped fritters) available year-round.

listings.name: Bar Tambayan
listings.content: Located in the northern reaches of Tetuán, this is arguably the best Filipino restaurant in Madrid, located in the heart of the city's Filipino neighborhood.

listings.name: Pastelería Mifer
listings.content: This unassuming bakery in Ciudad Lineal sells a wide variety of cakes and pastries, but they are best known for their award-winning torrijas (Spanish-style French toast) sold only during the run-up to Lent.

listings.name: Cafetería Nebraska
listings.content: Known throughout Madrid for their hot dogs, this Tetuán diner is the last of an old chain of restaurants dating back to 1955.

listings.name: Restaurante Bar Rodrigo
listings.content: Located behind the Mercado de Maravillas, this hidden gem in Tetuán serves affordable yet high-quality paellas that can compete with some of the best Madrid has to offer. Mostly patronized by locals, reservations are recommended, especially on weekends.
listings.address: Plaza de la Condesa de Gavia, 3

listings.name: Restaurante Malaysia
listings.content: Authentic Malaysian food served right in the heart of San Blas, with an extensive menu drawing from the diverse culinary traditions of Malaysia and its neighbors.

listings.name: Bar Jaén III
listings.content: An excellent tapas bar and restaurant. A nice place to enjoy Spanish food and lifestyle without spending too much. Being located just outside central Madrid, it's far from being a tourist trap and you can enjoy good food and true raciónes (portions). The pleasant owners are very willing to share stories about Madrid and Spain more generally. In summer time it has a superb terrace, within a stone's throw of the Olympic Stadium.

listings.name: Restaurante Samm
listings.content: A Chamartín institution lauded as having some of the best paellas (if not the best) in Madrid, but only if you bring more than two people by order of the proprietor. Walk-ins turned away from Casa Benigna on the other end of Chamartín are usually sent here. Frequented mainly by locals, prepare to be stared at by the wait staff if you are from out of town.

listings.name: Casa Nemesio
listings.content: Seafood.

listings.name: El Telégrafo
listings.content: Arguably the best seafood in Madrid.

listings.name: Restaurante Casa Benigna
listings.content: Owned by a Spanish-Norwegian family, this unassuming spot in Chamartín is known for serving traditional Spanish cuisine with a Nordic twist. Their paellas, served on custom-made copper pans, are reportedly among the best (if not the best) in Madrid, with prominent politicians, celebrities and businesspeople among their customers. Reservations recommended well in advance. Walk-ins are routinely turned away at the door and sent to Restaurante Samm on the other end of Chamartín.
